Summary:
A podcast-style customer interview with NovaInsights about their migration to Redwood Inference for core search and summarization features. Conversation covers why they chose Redwood, technical migration story, latency/cost wins, security considerations, and the business impact (faster time-to-market for features). Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: All right we're rolling um hey everyone thanks for joining today this is Jordan from Redwood marketing, uh excited to have NovaInsights with us for a customer interview - thanks for being here.
[00:08] Michael: Yeah thanks for having us, uh Michael here from NovaInsights, happy to chat.
[00:12] Priya: Hi all, Priya on the call too.
[00:14] Elena: Elena here - hello.
[00:16] Avery: Hey team, and Samira will be on for the tech bits.
[00:20] Samira: Hello hi.

[00:22] Jordan: Great, so this is more of a relaxed podcast format, we'll record and then Jordan will edit, but just before we dive can we confirm permissions to publish audio and a short case study?
[00:34] Michael: Yep we're good with that, pending a quick review of the transcript and the case write-up.
[00:38] Elena: Yep same, marketing sign-off on our side but happy to be featured.

[00:42] Jordan: Awesome, thanks. Quick warmup question: Mike, can you give a 30-second overview of NovaInsights and the problem you were solving?
[00:50] Michael: Sure, so NovaInsights is an analytics platform for customer feedback across multiple channels. We ingest text data from surveys, support tickets, and product reviews and then we run search and summarization to power our insights dashboard and alerts. The problem was our old inference stack started to show latency spikes and cost unpredictability as usage scaled, and we needed something that would give us consistent p50/p95 latency, better throughput and obvious unit economics.
[01:16] Jordan: Nice. Priya, what were the top technical criteria you were evaluating?
[01:21] Priya: Uh the main things were steady latency under load, simple integration with our existing AWS infra (VPC peering was important), model versioning and being able to A/B rollout model changes, and enterprise-grade security - SOC2-ish controls, KMS integration, and audit logs. Also we care about token cost per inference because we run millions of small requests.
[01:41] Samira: Quick follow up on that - when you say millions of small requests, were these mostly short prompts or a mixture with longer contexts?
[01:47] Priya: 80% short queries for search reranking and embeddings; 20% longer context summarization (1-2k tokens).

[01:52] Avery: Perfect - that matches what we saw in your onboarding telemetry. Could you talk through why you chose Redwood over other options?
[01:59] Michael: Yeah we evaluated hosted APIs like OpenAI and Anthropic for ease but the cost ramp was scary for our scale. We looked at self-hosted runtimes but didn't want to own the orchestration. Redwood hit the sweet spot: predictable latency in Dedicated mode, VPC options for security, and the Optimize tooling to tune batching and quantization recommendations which brought costs down. Also the team was responsive during the POC.
[02:25] Jordan: Nice, Priya did the POC go as expected?
[02:28] Priya: Mostly yes, there were a couple hiccups around our request patterns and KV cache warming - Samira was super helpful adjusting the batcher configuration and suggesting prefix caching. We also worked with the SEs to pick a quantized model variant for the short queries which reduced GPU cost per token substantially.
[02:46] Samira: I remember we ran a short benchmark where p95 latency improved from ~620ms to ~210ms for the 95th percentile on the short path after tuning.
[02:56] Michael: That matches our dashboard - our end users noticed faster load times and our error budget for SLAs is in a much healthier spot.

[03:02] Elena: From marketing side I'm curious about the business impact - any measurable metrics you can share?
[03:08] Michael: Sure we saw a ~2.1x improvement in throughput for the same GPU commit, and cost per 1k requests dropped roughly 35% after enabling batching and switching to the suggested quantized profile. Feature time-to-market also improved - we launched an insights digest product 3 weeks faster because we didn't have to build the orchestration layer.
[03:29] Jordan: Nice. Can you tell a quick anecdote about a user reaction?
[03:33] Michael: We had a trial customer who used the live summary widget, they said it was 'night and day' compared to our old system, the summaries were faster and more relevant.
[03:42] Elena: Love that quote, we may use it in the case study with permission.
[03:46] Michael: Yep go for it.

[03:48] Jordan: Let's shift to security - Priya you led that eval, what were the ask and outcome?
[03:53] Priya: We needed KMS integration, private network connectivity, and audit logs for compliance. Redwood's Private offering included a customer-managed VPC peering option and integrates with our AWS KMS for key rotation which met our policy. The compliance docs, SOC2 summary and architecture diagrams were helpful for the security team. We did request a small change to how logs are retained and Redwood accommodated that in the Dedicated contract.
[04:19] Samira: We logged the change request and the retention window was configurable for your account.
[04:25] Michael: That was important for legal sign-off.

[04:28] Jordan: Cool. Technical deep dive for a minute Samira you mentioned KV cache warming earlier can you explain that in lay terms for listeners?
[04:36] Samira: Sure - KV cache basically stores previous attention states for longer context so subsequent tokens can be generated faster. For workloads with similar prefixes we can reuse that state so the runtime doesn't redo expensive work. Warming just means we prime that cache for typical prefixes so the first real request benefits. Novainsights had a lot of repeatable short queries which were a good fit.
[04:57] Priya: The other win was batching for tiny requests; Redwood's smart batching kept tail latency low while still getting the benefits of larger batches.
[05:05] Jordan: Any funny mis-transcriptions in the onboarding docs, Mike?
[05:07] Michael: (laughs) Yeah one doc had 'KV cash' instead of 'KV cache' and our finance team thought we were spending money on caches.

[05:15] Jordan: (laughs) Classic. Switching gears what's been the support experience like?
[05:20] Michael: Great. AE and SE were responsive during the ramp, and the Redwood Console dashboards gave us the visibility we needed. The one-off support for a model rollback was handled overnight.
[05:30] Priya: Also the troubleshooting playbook for private deployment had clear steps which reduced our ops time.

[05:36] Jordan: For listeners curious about migration, how long did the end-to-end migration take?
[05:41] Michael: From initial POC to production it was about 6 weeks total. The POC was two weeks, integration and testing three weeks, and final cutover took a few days.
[05:51] Jordan: That's pretty quick. Was there a canary or A/B rollout?
[05:54] Priya: We did a canary with 10% traffic for a week then ramped to 100% after verification. Redwood's rollout controls made that easy.

[06:03] Jordan: Any remaining pain points or feature asks?
[06:06] Michael: We'd like better multi-region replication for lower cross-region latency in APAC eventually. Also a little more visibility into kernel-level metrics would be nice for deep perf analysis.
[06:18] Samira: Noted - we have a roadmap item for enhanced perf telemetry and multi-region routing improvements.

[06:24] Elena: On the marketing side let's talk assets - Jordan, we want the case study to highlight the numbers you mentioned, include the quote about 'night and day' and a short blurb from Priya about security.
[06:36] Jordan: Sounds good, we'll draft and send for approvals.

[06:40] Michael: Quick note - please anonymize any raw request samples in the public assets.
[06:45] Jordan: Absolutely - we'll scrub anything PII.

[06:47] Jordan: Last set of quick questions for the podcast: Priya, any advice for other ML teams contemplating a move like yours?
[06:54] Priya: Start with a short POC focused on your p95 latency and cost per inference metrics, and involve security early. Also instrument metrics from day one so you can make data-driven tweaks to batching and caching.
[07:07] Michael: I'd add - evaluate both hosted and dedicated flows; sometimes a hybrid approach is the right fit.

[07:13] Jordan: Great. We're almost out of time, any final thoughts?
[07:16] Elena: Thank you, happy to help with marketing artifacts.
[07:19] Michael: Appreciate the partnership - it's sped up our roadmap.
[07:22] Jordan: Awesome, we'll wrap up. Recap of next steps: Jordan will send edited audio and transcript for approval; Samira to provide benchmarking chart and short note on tuning; marketing to draft case study and share with Elena. Anything to add?
[07:36] Priya: No that's it.
[07:38] Michael: All good.

[07:40] Jordan: Perfect, thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email. Bye!
